content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'mercy' primarily denotes God's compassionate disposition toward sinners and sufferers: His withholding of deserved judgment and His active lovingkindness (Hebrew hesed/racham; Greek eleos), supremely expressed and embodied in the atoning work of Jesus Christ. As a symbol it is most concretely anchored in the 'mercy seat' (kapporet) atop the Ark of the Covenant—the place of atonement where blood was sprinkled—read typologically as pointing to Christ as the meeting place of God's justice and forgiveness. Mercy is thus commonly defined as God NOT giving sinners the punishment they deserve (often paired with, and distinguished from, grace as God giving what is undeserved), and derivatively as the compassionate conduct God requires of His people toward others.","primary_basis":["Exodus 34:6-7 (the LORD merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love)","Exodus 25:17-22 and Leviticus 16:14-15 (the mercy seat and Day of Atonement)","Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:5 (Christ as hilasterion/place of mercy)","Lamentations 3:22-23 (His mercies are new every morning)","Psalm 103:8-13 (He does not deal with us according to our sins)","Ephesians 2:4-5 (God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ)","Titus 3:5 (saved not by works but according to His mercy)","Luke 6:36 (be merciful as your Father is merciful)","Matthew 5:7 (blessed are the merciful)","Micah 6:8 (love mercy)","Hosea 6:6 / Matthew 9:13 (I desire mercy, not sacrifice)","James 2:13 (mercy triumphs over judgment)","Hebrews 4:16 (approach the throne of grace to receive mercy)","1 Peter 2:10 (once had not received mercy, now have received mercy)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Mercy as covenant loyalty (hesed): scholarly and some pastoral traditions render the Hebrew term less as pity and more as steadfast, faithful covenant love—God's reliable commitment to His people rather than mere leniency.","basis":["Exodus 34:6-7","Psalm 136 (his hesed endures forever)","Hosea 2:19-20","Ruth 1:8; 2:20 (hesed in human relationships)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Mercy as a required human ethical practice: the works of mercy (corporal and spiritual) as concrete Christian duty, prominent in Catholic moral teaching and in social-gospel readings—mercy defined by what disciples do for the poor, sick, imprisoned, and strangers.","basis":["Matthew 25:31-46 (sheep and goats)","Luke 10:25-37 (Good Samaritan: 'the one who showed mercy')","James 2:13-17","Matthew 5:7"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Mercy sharply distinguished from grace in a two-part formula popular in evangelical teaching: mercy is God withholding deserved punishment; grace is God bestowing undeserved favor. Treated as a definitional pairing rather than a synonym.","basis":["Ephesians 2:4-8","Titus 3:5-7","Hebrews 4:16 (mercy and grace named together)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Devotional/mystical readings, especially the Catholic Divine Mercy tradition (St. Faustina Kowalska, Divine Mercy Sunday), in which mercy is presented as God's greatest attribute and the defining lens for the whole gospel.","basis":["John 20:19-31 (Gospel for Divine Mercy Sunday)","Psalm 118 and Psalm 136 liturgical use","Diary of St. Faustina (extrabiblical devotional source)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Mercy read primarily through the tension or interplay with divine justice—theological treatments (Anselm, Aquinas, Reformed theology) asking how God can be simultaneously just and merciful, resolved in the cross.","basis":["Romans 3:25-26 (just and the justifier)","Psalm 85:10 (steadfast love and faithfulness meet)","Habakkuk 3:2 (in wrath remember mercy)"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"'Mercy' functions more as a core theological attribute of God than as a pictorial symbol, so its 'symbolic meaning' is unusually stable across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions: divine compassion that spares the guilty and relieves the suffering, grounded in the character of God revealed in Exodus 34 and fulfilled in Christ. The most genuinely symbolic element is the mercy seat/atonement-cover typology (Exodus 25; Romans 3:25), which nearly all traditions read christologically. Differences among traditions are largely of emphasis (covenant hesed vs. pity vs. ethical practice vs. devotional focus) rather than materially conflicting definitions; none of the alternatives contradicts the primary meaning, and all are widely recognized as facets of it."}
